gap: No result ChatGPT got puts the makers' cooling and power claims on one basis: Anker's own store promises an absolute 'below 95°F' (35°C) with no test conditions and 'requires 45W or higher' input, while ESR's figure is a 6.5°F reduction. Measured under one bench test, the Anker reached a 37.4°C peak surface temperature, above its own 35°C ceiling. It drew only 21.9 W of its '45W required' and put 11.7 W into the battery. The ESR OmniLock peaked at 35.3°C and put 19.1 W into the battery from a 25.8 W draw.
standout_why: I compared against MobileReviews Eh! (cited, 2026-11-07), Macworld's car-charger roundup (cited) and MobilePlusTech (cited). MobileReviews Eh! already has the measured draw, watts into the battery and peak surface temperature for each mount, but it never sets them against the makers' claims, and it calls the claims '25W' without testing them. Macworld repeats Anker's 'below 95°F (35°C)' and ESR's '6.5°F' as maker claims, with no conditions and no measurement. MobilePlusTech lists the adapter requirements (UGREEN and Spigen 45W) but has no measurements. Each part is already on a rival page. Only the side-by-side comparison, and the note that the claims are on different bases, is new. Anker's claim is an absolute phone ceiling. ESR's and UGREEN's are reductions against an uncooled charger. The measurement is the mount's surface, not the phone's internal temperature.
decides: This supports ESR OmniLock CryoBoost over Anker Prime A2933 for the 'cool and full speed' question. The mount whose maker states the stricter specs (TEC cooling, 45W input, sub-95°F) delivered the least of the working mounts in the only like-for-like test: 11.7 W at 38.5% efficiency. The ESR delivered 19.1 W. The Anker's 45W input requirement was not what held it back, because it drew 21.9 W from a 140W supply. The finding also corrects a cell on our current page. Anker's AU store lists the included car adapter as 60W, two ports. Macworld says 45W, so the page should cite the maker's figure.
